dialogues.text: Welcome to Pool Trader!
Today you're going to learn how to find your way around a small market of digital assets.
A market?
Do I need to know about trading or cryptocurrencies to play?
No. We'll start from scratch.
First you'll understand what you're buying and selling.
Then we'll see how all of this happens on the blockchain.
And finally you'll learn how to take advantage of market movements.
Let's start with the most important thing.
In this game you'll come across two tokens used on an ERC-20 network: WBTC (<sprite="BTC" index=0>) and ETH (<sprite="ETH" index=0>).
Okay… but what exactly is a token?
A token is basically a digital asset that can be transferred between users.
It can also be used inside a system.
It can represent many things, from ideas or jokes to physical assets.
It can also represent shares, or even other cryptocurrencies.
You can think of it as a digital chip.
Okay... I get it, but how am I supposed to use those tokens?
Very simple. You're just going to swap them.
To do that you'll have to pay a small charge that we call a fee.
Fee? Sounds familiar from the minigame we played before.
Exactly!
A fee is a charge you pay to operate on the blockchain.
It's a variable rate, so it can change over time.
But I don't have any money, how am I going to pay that?
Don't worry, I've brought a couple of bags for you.
With these bags you'll be able to make your first swaps.
And you can always get more during your conversion turn.
These bags are how you swap tokens.
Without them you won't be able to buy or sell, so make sure you always have a few with you.
Also, the coins you've collected in your final result will be turned into new bags.
And at a generous rate.
Okay, tell me more about who swaps those tokens.
Around here, some people want certain tokens and others want different ones.
For example, someone might have WBTC (<sprite="BTC" index=0>), the orange coin, and want ETH (<sprite="ETH" index=0>).
Someone else might have ETH (<sprite="ETH" index=0>), the blue coin, and prefer WBTC (<sprite="BTC" index=0>).
And why would anyone want to swap a token?
They might want to use it, keep it or swap it later.
Or they might simply think its value could go up.
You don't need to know each person's exact reason.
What matters is that different people want to swap different digital assets.
Those digital assets are the tokens.
So this exists because not everyone wants the same coins?
And we need to swap them?
Exactly!
What you need to understand is that tokens are digital assets whose price fluctuates.
People swap them because they have different needs, goals or expectations about their value.
And that's the key thing you need to remember!
Okay, I know what I'm swapping. But… with whom?
Here's the interesting part.
In real life, if you want to buy a ring, you have to find someone else who'll sell it to you.
It doesn't work quite like that here. You don't need to personally find someone who wants to make the opposite swap.
All of this is thanks to the liquidity pool.
Imagine the pool as a place with two big reserves, like this one:
Each one holds a different token so users can swap them with each other.
And who puts those assets into the reserve?
Liquidity providers.
They're users who contribute assets to the pool so others can make swaps.
So the liquidity providers put in the assets…
And the traders use them to swap.
Exactly. You can think of it as a book-swap shop.
The liquidity providers fill the shelves, which are the pool's reserves.
Notice how there's now the same amount of each type of token in both reserves.
Traders come in to buy and sell, leaving some 'books' and taking others.
And the bookshop, which would be the liquidity pool, makes those swaps possible.
And do liquidity providers do all this for free?
Not at all.
In a real system, providing liquidity requires rewards for every swap.
Going back to the bookshop example, think of these fees as a small cost.
The bookshop owner keeps that cost for providing the place where you swap books, and it's higher the more books they have available.
However, in this minigame, to keep things simple, we won't take them into account.
I see, so the reserves...
Those reserves are called a liquidity pool, remember.
Alright, so the liquidity pool provides the... books?
Tokens. What gets swapped are tokens, go on...
Okay, the liquidity pool provides the tokens, and the... users? swap them.
Very good! The users who do this are called traders, remember?
I see, so the liquidity pool provides the tokens so traders can swap them.
Exactly! The most important thing is that a liquidity pool is a reserve of tokens kept by users called liquidity providers.
It depends on them to work. Thanks to them, traders can make swaps.
This is blowing my mind. And how do those swaps you're talking about work?
HAHAHA, I love your questions.
Let's take two tokens. You have WBTC (<sprite="BTC" index=0>)
And you want to get ETH (<sprite="ETH" index=0>)
The price is currently 1 BTC (<sprite="BTC" index=0>) for 1 ETH (<sprite="ETH" index=0>)
You'll press the sell button, giving BTC (<sprite="BTC" index=0>) to the pool
Go ahead, press it
Very good! Notice how, in return, you receive ETH (<sprite="ETH" index=0>).
So it's like exchanging one currency for another.
Yes, but there's an important difference.
The pool doesn't have an infinite amount of assets.
Every time someone buys an asset, the amount available in the pool changes.
Notice how the amounts are no longer equal
And does that affect the price?
Exactly.
Imagine lots of people are buying ETH (<sprite="ETH" index=0>).
Each swap reduces the amount of ETH (<sprite="ETH" index=0>) available in the pool.
And increases the amount of the asset in the other reserve that they use to buy
That's why the price changes. Notice there's now more BTC (<sprite="BTC" index=0>) than ETH (<sprite="ETH" index=0>)
That's because you deposited one BTC coin (<sprite="BTC" index=0>) and took out ALMOST one ETH coin (<sprite="ETH" index=0>)
Notice you didn't take out a full 1 ETH (<sprite="ETH" index=0>).
That's because there are few enough coins that, when you buy 1, your effective price isn't exactly 1:1 but slightly lower, 1:0.93
Notice how the overall price has changed too
This is a bit complex, why does the price change so much?
Think of the pool as a container.
If you take from one side and add to the other, the balance changes.
This means every swap has different conditions.
In other words, each swap will pay a slightly different price than the previous one
So I can't assume BTC (<sprite="BTC" index=0>) always costs the same.
Correct. Even if sometimes the difference is small, the price is rarely exactly the same as before
But you don't need to memorise a formula to play either.
Just remember this rule:
Every swap changes the state of the pool and, therefore, the price.
So my own trades can change the market.
Yes. And that will be very important.
What matters is that every swap changes the amounts of assets in the pool.
And those changes make the price move.
The fuller the reserves are, the smaller these price swings will be.
If, on the other hand, they're nearly empty, a small swap can change the price drastically.
Remember, these are the reserves
So I can control the price if I make enough swaps.
Not so fast.
You're not the only one trading.
There are more people?
Lots. They're called traders, remember?
During the game, these traders will also make swaps.
Some will buy BTC (<sprite="BTC" index=0>).
Others will buy ETH (<sprite="ETH" index=0>).
And their trades will also change the pool and, as a result, the price.
So the price can change even if I do nothing.
Exactly.
And that means you can't control it.
You can only react to what's happening.
So I have to watch what the others do.
Correct, but above all how the pool's proportions change.
Because a good opportunity can show up right after another trader's move.
Your goal isn't to predict every move.
It's to learn to recognise when you have an opportunity to take advantage of and get more tokens.
What matters is that you're playing against other traders, who also change the pool's proportions.
And that creates opportunities for you.
Okay, now I understand the pool and the swaps.
But how does everything work during a game?
This is where our turn system comes in.
Each turn has four phases, always in this order.
First: Traders.
Then: Conversion.
Next: Player swap.
And finally: Liquidity providers.
And then it starts again?
Exactly.
Once the four phases are over, a new turn begins.
Enough explaining, try it yourself:
